title: A later break on the will
body: Writers in this library from Hermas through Lactantius generally treat human beings as capable of deliberate choice — praised or blamed for what they choose. Augustine’s late teaching that the fallen will cannot turn to God without prior grace sits notably apart from that earlier pattern. Julian of Eclanum’s surviving arguments fight to keep the earlier emphasis.

title: Guilt by birth vs guilt by deed
body: Earlier topical excerpts here stress disobedience, luxury, and personal turning from God — not a damning guilt transmitted by generation alone. Augustine’s doctrine of original guilt inherited at birth is the sharp later claim; Julian’s replies deny that marriage and birth transmit a sinful nature.

title: Assistance or remaking of the will
body: Ante-Nicene voices in this seed set speak of God’s help alongside a will that still acts and is formed. Augustine’s later framing makes grace the prior remaking without which the will cannot begin the good. That is the rupture Explore is meant to make visible — not a score of who was “right.”

title: Faith that obeys, from exhortation to martyrdom
body: Across these 118 excerpts the ante-Nicene pattern is steady: Irenaeus and Origen root faith itself in free decision; Tertullian and Commodian join it to repentance, alms, and daily warfare against vice; Lactantius, Arnobius, and Minucius defend believing as a reasonable choice crowned by the martyrs’ patience. Novatian’s rule-of-faith passages fix what is believed while the rest press how believers must live. The later Augustinian note — faith as a gift worked in the will before any choosing — has no voice in this corpus; the contrast entry carries that side alone.

title: Made in image, yet Arnobius dissents
body: From Barnabas to Lactantius the excerpts agree that God made the human being in his image, and Tertullian traces the soul itself to God's breath — simple, intelligent, and ruling from conception. Arnobius breaks ranks inside the same library: souls are not God's offspring or immortal by nature, and men differ from beasts hardly at all. Novatian meanwhile puts 'image' on Christ the Son, the visible image of the invisible Father — a second use of the word, not a second opinion about man.

title: Living gifts, contested prophecy, then quieter signs
body: 100–220: Didache and Hermas test itinerant prophets by life and stay-rules; Justin and Irenaeus say healings, foreknowledge, tongues, and prophecy still run in the churches; Hippolytus names Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla as a rival prophetic circle. 325: Eusebius preserves both ongoing χάρισμα and the anti-ecstatic rule of true prophecy. 350–390: Cyril refuses Paraclete monopolies; Basil reads 1 Cor 12 as Spirit-ordered offices and gifts; Chrysostom asks why baptismal tongues common then are not now. 426–427: Augustine says Acts-style tongues and shadow-healings ceased, yet miracles in Christ’s name still happen with less fame. 594: Gregory still collects living signs, but ranks converting a sinner above raising the dead. That is the real 0–800 arc — not silence after the apostles, and not a flat modern charismatic map either.
